title: Two words for one thing
goal: Match Ottoman words with their modern partners, and choose the one that fits the tone.

intro.text: For many things Turkish has two words: an Ottoman one from Arabic or Persian, and one from the language reform of the 1930s. In some pairs one word won (*mektep* gave way to *okul*); in others both live on with a different tone (*cevap*, *yanıt*).

vocab.en: dictionary (dated; TDK prefers sözlük); once also word
word (the Öz Türkçe partner of kelime)
answer, reply (a little more written than cevap)
matter, issue; the point (mesele şu: the thing is)
freedom, liberty (more historical or solemn than özgürlük)
exam (old-fashioned; today sınav); a trial, an ordeal
native Turkish words; the movement to use them

exercises.question: Which pair has a clear winner today, with the Ottoman word marked old-fashioned?

why.1: Both are alive: *cevap* is the everyday word, *yanıt* a little more written.
why.2: Both are standard; *sözcük* is the usual term in grammar books.
why.3: Both are alive, and *mesele* also means **the point**: *Mesele şu.*

exercises.explain: TDK marks *sual* as old-fashioned (*esk.*) and sends the reader to *soru*.

exercises.text: Dedem tayyare derdi, biz ___ diyoruz; o lügat derdi, biz ___ diyoruz.
exercises.en: My grandfather used to say tayyare, and we say …; he used to say lügat, and we say …

accept: uçak
sözlük

exercises.hint: Both modern words are A1 vocabulary: a plane and a dictionary.
exercises.explain: *Tayyare* gave way to *uçak*, and *lügat* to *sözlük*: in both pairs the Öz Türkçe word won.

exercises.question: *Bu hastalık bütün aile için ağır bir imtihan oldu.* What does *imtihan* mean here?

why.1: For school, Turkish says *sınav*; *imtihan* lives on in the figurative sense.
why.3: The illness is the trial: nothing is being tested in a laboratory.

exercises.explain: TDK gives *imtihan* two senses: an exam (it prefers *sınav*) and, figuratively, a hard situation that tests you.

exercises.en: My grandfather still calls school mektep.

exercises.question: A friend texts you: *Sualimi anladın mı?* How does it sound?
options: Old-fashioned on purpose: a joke, or a great-grandfather's voice

why.1: The everyday sentence is *Sorumu anladın mı?*
why.2: Nothing rude: *sual* is a polite old word.
why.3: Children say *soru*: *sual* belongs to their great-grandparents.

exercises.explain: TDK marks *sual* as old-fashioned. In a text message it sounds like a deliberate joke.

exercises.task: Your grandfather's old letter is full of Ottoman words. Rewrite it in today's Turkish, replacing every word that has a modern partner. (*İmtihan vermek* means **to pass an exam**.)
exercises.source: Sevgili torunum, mektebin nasıl gidiyor? İmtihanlarını verdin mi? Muallimine benden selam söyle. Tayyare ile geleceğini duydum; seni karşılamaya geleceğim.
models: Sevgili torunum, okulun nasıl gidiyor? Sınavlarını verdin mi? Öğretmenine benden selam söyle. Uçakla geleceğini duydum; seni karşılamaya geleceğim.
checklist: The rest is already modern: *torun*, *selam söylemek*, *karşılamak* stay
